name: Foot orthotic insoles
lead: Foot orthotic insoles, also called shoe inserts, foot orthoses or orthotics, are removable supports placed inside footwear. They are sold for comfort, arch support, pain relief, orthopaedic correction, athletic performance and, in some products, added height.[1] For appearance, the relevant uses are the ones that change how someone stands and walks: a heel lift raises the wearer by the thickness of the insert while hiding the added height inside the shoe, and corrective insoles are used to even out a leg-length difference or support the arch so that gait and stance look more balanced.[1][20]

They are either custom made from a cast or scan of the foot or bought ready made. Medical uses are the best studied, notably heel pain from plantar fasciitis, where reviews list orthotics among first-line conservative measures.[1][2][3] A 2018 meta-analysis of 19 randomised trials found orthoses reduced heel pain more than sham devices in the medium term, and a 2008 Cochrane review found custom orthoses helped several painful foot conditions.[11][12] Evidence for medical use is described as mixed, and no studies were found of insoles as a posture, gait-appearance or height tool in people without a foot condition.[1]
The brand most associated with the category in the United States is Dr. Scholl's, founded in 1906 by the podiatrist William Mathias Scholl.[13]

paras: Custom inserts are made by an orthotics laboratory from a plaster cast, foam impression or 3D scan, with digital scans used to drive CNC machines. Firm supports hold a fixed position, flexible supports move with the foot while supporting the arch, and soft supports of foam, gel or similar materials mainly absorb shock. Ready-made pads and heel inserts are also sold. Wikipedia reports that none of the three fitting methods produces a proper fit more than about 80 percent of the time, and that little research guides which type or material suits which patient.[1]

Orthotics as a field is broader than insoles and includes ankle-foot orthoses and braces for other body regions. In the United States an orthotist needs a prescription from a licensed healthcare provider, while in the United Kingdom orthotists often accept referrals without one.[21] Grokipedia describes the history of the field, from ancient splints to the plastics of the 1960s and 3D printing, but that history concerns orthotics generally rather than insoles.[4]

Wikipedia describes elevator shoes as shoes with thickened insoles or lifts under the heels that make the wearer look taller, with the added height hidden inside the shoe rather than visible as with high-heeled shoes; the lift can be made of plastic, wood or rubber.[20] A 1977 newspaper article titled 'Elevator Shoes A Boost' and a 2013 Smithsonian Magazine piece on how to be taller are among the sources Wikipedia cites.[20] Removable heel inserts sold for height follow the same principle in a separable form, and Wikipedia lists height enhancement among the purposes shoe inserts are sold for.[1]

Heel raises are also used clinically. In a randomised trial published in 2021, heel lifts were compared with calf eccentric exercise for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy.[9] Leg-length discrepancy and its effects on gait are the subject of a 2002 review, and heel lifts and insoles are one way such differences are compensated.[22]

William Mathias Scholl, a podiatrist, started the Dr. Scholl's brand in 1906 and is credited with designing over 1,000 foot-care products; the company was named to the Fortune 500 in 1971, the year it went public.[13] Ownership has since passed through Schering-Plough (1979), Merck (2009), Bayer (2014) and Yellow Wood Partners, which bought the brand from Bayer in 2019 for about $585 million and reunited it with the international Scholl business in 2021.[13]

A review in American Family Physician describes plantar fasciitis as a self-limiting cause of heel pain with excessive foot pronation as a risk factor.[2] A 2025 Danish review states that first-line treatment is conservative, including unloading, stretching, eccentric exercise, suitable footwear and orthotics, with about 90 percent of patients improving within a year.[3] A Cureus review of diagnosis and management frameworks covers the same condition.[5] Wikipedia reports that plantar fasciitis accounts for about 80 percent of heel pain, that customised orthoses can offer short-term relief typically after about eight weeks, and that no single treatment is established as clearly superior.[23]

A paediatric review says flatfoot in children is usually a benign variant and that treatment is indicated for symptomatic cases.[6] Reviews of Morton's neuroma list orthotics among treatment options.[7] Wikipedia says medical use is criticised for weak evidence, that podiatrists often prescribe different orthoses for the same patient, and that patients often report short-term comfort gains.[1]

For mechanism, a 2010 systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 papers by Mills and colleagues found that posted non-moulded orthoses reduced peak rearfoot eversion by about 2 degrees in uninjured people, and that moulded orthoses reduced loading rate and vertical impact force, while evidence for neuromotor effects was the least conclusive.[14]

A 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 randomised trials (1,660 participants) of foot orthoses for plantar heel pain found no benefit at 0 to 6 weeks on very low-quality evidence, a greater pain reduction than sham orthoses at 7 to 12 weeks on moderate-quality evidence (standardised mean difference -0.27) without functional improvement, and no benefit at 13 to 52 weeks. Custom and prefabricated orthoses performed the same at every time point.[11]

A 2008 Cochrane review of 11 trials (1,332 participants) found custom-made orthoses were effective for painful pes cavus, rearfoot pain in rheumatoid arthritis, foot pain in juvenile idiopathic arthritis and painful hallux valgus, while evidence for plantar fasciitis was unclear; orthoses were safe across the studies.[12] A 2010 systematic review of seven studies on patellofemoral pain found limited evidence that prefabricated orthoses gave greater short-term improvement than flat inserts.[15]

A 2013 JAMA meta-analysis of 12 trials of lateral wedge insoles for medial knee osteoarthritis found less pain than controls overall, but no meaningful effect in the seven trials using a neutral insole comparator, and the authors concluded the evidence did not support their use for this indication.[16]

A randomised trial of 48 patients with plantar fasciitis gave all participants shoe inserts and compared plantar-specific stretching with high-load strength training, with the strength group faring better at follow-up. This tested exercise, not the inserts themselves.[8] A pragmatic randomised equivalence trial compared heel lifts with calf eccentric exercise for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy.[9] A randomised trial examined different foot orthoses and gait mechanics in people with rheumatoid arthritis.[10]
No published trials were found of insoles used for height, posture or appearance in healthy people.

The Cochrane review reported orthoses as safe across the studies it analysed.[12] Wikipedia notes that effects vary by patient and no standard personalisation practice exists.[1] Clinicians treating plantar fasciitis typically combine insoles with stretching, exercise and footwear changes rather than using insoles alone.[3][8]

Wikipedia lists height enhancement among the reasons shoe inserts are sold, and elevator-style inserts are one of the low-cost, reversible ways people add apparent height without changing their bodies.[1][20] The inserts add height only while worn and are limited by how much heel room the shoe has.

lore.intro: Insoles are marketed and discussed as a way to add height, fix alignment and relieve foot pain; the claims below are drawn from how sellers, clinicians and Wikipedia describe them.[1][20]

claims.claim: Elevator insoles add height without anyone noticing.
claims.believers: Sellers and wearers describe heel lifts as a hidden way to gain apparent height, because the lift sits inside the shoe.[20]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the lift as hiding added height from observers; no studies have measured how observers perceive insole-added height.[20]

claims.claim: Custom orthotics work better than ready-made ones.
claims.believers: Prescribers of custom devices point to individual casts or scans as a better fit.[1]
claims.experts: A 2018 meta-analysis found custom and prefabricated orthoses performed the same for plantar heel pain at every time point.[11]

claims.believers: Patients often report short-term comfort improvements.[1]
claims.experts: A 2018 meta-analysis found moderate-quality evidence of greater pain reduction than sham at 7 to 12 weeks, with unclear clinical importance.[11]

claims.believers: Podiatrists prescribe orthoses to hold the arch or heel in a set position.[1]
claims.experts: A 2010 meta-analysis found posted orthoses reduced peak rearfoot eversion by about 2 degrees in uninjured people.[14]

claims.believers: They are marketed as a conservative knee-pain measure.[16]
claims.experts: A 2013 JAMA meta-analysis found no meaningful effect when compared with neutral insoles.[16]

claims.claim: Insoles replace exercise for heel pain.
claims.believers: Insoles are often tried first because they are simple to use.[2]
claims.experts: A randomised trial found high-load strength training improved outcomes beyond stretching in patients who all wore inserts.[8]

card.summary: Shoe inserts sold for comfort, gait and height; evidence is for heel pain, with none found for looks or posture.
card.note: Medical evidence is mixed and none was found for appearance, posture or height use in healthy people.

quick.overview:
Orthotic insoles are removable supports for the shoe, either custom made from a foot scan or bought ready made. They are sold for comfort, arch support, pain relief and, in some products, extra height.
Their best-studied use is heel pain from plantar fasciitis. No studies were found of them for posture, gait appearance or height in people without a foot problem.
quick.mechanism: They redistribute load across the foot and may hold the arch or heel in a set position; heel inserts also raise the heel by a small amount.
quick.risks: Reviews describe mixed evidence for medical use and inconsistent fit across methods. Harms of insoles themselves are not well documented, but clinicians treat the underlying conditions with several measures, not insoles alone.

chain: Raises the heel or supports the arch and foot position
Slightly taller standing frame or more even stance and gait
angle.text: A heel-lift insole adds height equal to its thickness while worn and cannot be seen from outside the shoe. Supportive or corrective insoles are used to redistribute load across the foot and to compensate for a leg-length difference, which people use to look and walk more evenly.
